source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: Best use of test-time compute depends on question difficulty. Easy questions gain more from sequential revision; hard ones from parallel sampling or PRM tree search. An adaptive compute-optimal policy beats best-of-N.
numbers: Compute-optimal policy matches best-of-N with about 4x less compute (revisions and PRM search). FLOPs-matched against a 14x larger pretrained model: test-time compute wins on easy and intermediate questions; on the hardest questions pretraining wins. PaLM 2-S*, MATH.
quote: scaling test-time computation can already serve to be more preferable to scaling up pretraining
limits: Difficulty bins come from the base model's own pass rate (needs sampling to estimate). Only MATH and PaLM 2. Very hard questions show little gain.
agent_relevance: Direct basis for G12: budget by difficulty. Use a cheap difficulty estimate at the S0 gate; spend little on easy items and do not pour compute into hopeless ones.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Coverage (any sample correct) grows near log-linearly with number of samples over orders of magnitude, fits an exponentiated power law. Where an automatic verifier exists, coverage turns into real accuracy.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite: DeepSeek-Coder-V2 15.9% (1 sample) to 56% (250 samples), above single-sample SOTA 43%. CodeContests Gemma-2B: 0.02% to 7.1% at 10,000 samples. MATH Llama-3-8B: coverage 82.9% (100 samples) to 98.44% (10,000), but majority vote or reward model only 40.50% to 41.41% over the same range.
limits: Gap between coverage and selected-answer accuracy is the catch: without a reliable verifier, extra samples are wasted. Power law is empirical, not guaranteed.
agent_relevance: Sampling more only pays if the agent has a real checker (tests, proof, calculation). Without one, spend on verification design, not more samples.

source: Wu, Sun, Li, Welleck, Yang (2024) Inference Scaling Laws: An Empirical Analysis of Compute-Optimal Inference
finding: At a fixed inference FLOPs budget a smaller model with more samples can beat a larger model, until the small model saturates. Their tree search REBASE beats plain sampling and MCTS on the compute-accuracy trade-off.
numbers: Llemma-7B beats Llemma-34B until about 128 samples; Llemma-7B + REBASE beats Llemma-34B with standard majority vote at all budgets (MATH500, GSM8K). Pythia GSM8K curves show saturation of small models.
limits: Accuracy saturates at a limit set by the model's output probabilities. Math only; same Llemma-34B reward model used for all runs.
agent_relevance: Cheap-and-many is good only up to a ceiling. Escalate to a stronger model or a different method when samples stop adding new answers.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Can 1B LLM Surpass 405B LLM? Rethinking Compute-Optimal Test-Time Scaling
finding: Best test-time strategy depends jointly on the policy model, the PRM and the problem difficulty. With the right strategy, small models beat much larger ones on math.
numbers: Reported in abstract: 1B beats 405B on MATH-500; 0.5B beats GPT-4o; 3B beats 405B; 7B beats o1 and DeepSeek-R1 (MATH-500 and AIME24). PRMs 1.5B to 72B, policies 0.5B to 72B, two families.
limits: Needs a good PRM per task; claims are for math with a trained PRM. Comparisons to big models use extra inference compute for the small model.
agent_relevance: Strategy must be chosen per model and per difficulty; a fixed recipe (always N=16) is a poor default.

source: Chen, Davis, Hanin, Bailis, Stoica, Zaharia, Zou (2024) Are More LLM Calls All You Need? Towards Scaling Laws of Compound Inference Systems
finding: Majority-vote accuracy can rise and then fall as the number of calls grows. Cause: more votes help easy queries and hurt hard queries (where a wrong answer is the plurality). The optimal number of calls can be predicted from a small sample.
numbers: Non-monotone scaling across several language tasks for Vote and Filter-Vote; theory gives the conditions via the mix of easy and hard queries.
quote: more LM calls lead to higher performance on easy queries, but lower performance on hard queries
limits: Theory assumes a simple easy/hard split; real difficulty is continuous. Older model class (GPT-3.5 era).
agent_relevance: Argues for a per-item call count and for stopping rules, not one big N for everything.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling
finding: Training on only 1,000 curated traces plus budget forcing (suppress end of thinking, append Wait) gives clear sequential scaling. Sequential beats parallel majority voting on the base model.
numbers: s1-32B: AIME24 50% to 57% with forcing beyond training length; up to 27% above o1-preview on MATH and AIME24. Ablation (AIME24): 1K-random 36.7, 59K-full 33.3, s1K higher. 26 minutes of training. Forcing 2/4/6 times: gains flatten at six.
quote: Scaling test-time compute on the base model via majority voting cannot catch up with the performance of s1-32B
limits: Gains flatten and loops appear when stopping is suppressed too often; context window caps scaling. AIME24 has 30 problems, so confidence intervals are wide (paper reports intervals of tens of points on ablations).
agent_relevance: Forcing a second look helps up to a point (one or two rounds). Build a hard cap on extra rounds.

source: Gema et al. (2025) Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute (TMLR)
finding: On designed tasks, longer reasoning lowers accuracy. Five failure modes: distraction (Claude), overfitting to framing (o-series), drift to spurious features, losing focus on constraint tracking, amplified self-preservation statements.
numbers: Misleading Math/Python counting: 2,500 questions each, 1-5 distractors. Claude Opus 4 falls from near 100% to about 80% with extended thinking; o3 stays stable or rises; DeepSeek R1 flat on some tasks, drops on others. Zebra puzzles: R1 drops most. Sonnet 4 non-self-preservation rate 60% to 47%.
limits: Tasks are built to fail; effect depends on model and on budget method (controlled vs natural); few-shot examples help. Many curves are flat or noisy.
agent_relevance: Evidence for a hard stop and a no-think path on simple items: more thinking can hurt when distractors are present. Strip irrelevant context before reasoning.

source: Stroebl, Kapoor, Narayanan (2024) Inference Scaling fLaws: The Limits of LLM Resampling with Imperfect Verifiers
finding: With a verifier that sometimes passes wrong answers, resampling has a hard accuracy ceiling set by the false positive rate. Weak models cannot match strong ones by sampling.
numbers: HumanEval+/MBPP+ used as ground truth against HumanEval/MBPP tests as verifier: single-sample accuracy correlates strongly with false-positive rate. With a cost for false positives the best number of attempts is often below 10, sometimes zero.
limits: Coding only; depends on test-suite coverage. False-positive code also scored worse on style.
agent_relevance: Verifier quality caps the useful budget. Cap retries; test the verifier on held-out cases.

source: Hassid et al. (2025) Don't Overthink It: Preferring Shorter Thinking Chains for Improved LLM Reasoning
finding: Within one question, shorter reasoning chains are more often correct than the longest. short-m@k (stop when the first m of k parallel chains finish, then vote) matches or beats majority voting with fewer tokens.
numbers: Shortest chain up to 34.5% more accurate than longest for the same question; short-1@k up to 40% fewer thinking tokens; short-3@k beats majority voting at all budgets with up to 33% less wall time. Fine-tuning on short chains beats long or random chains.
limits: Correlation within a question, not cause: confused paths may run long. Needs parallel generation.
agent_relevance: A cheap rule: when sampling several, trust early finishers; very long chains signal confusion.

source: Wang et al. (2022) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
finding: Sample many chains and take the majority answer. Large, consistent gains over greedy chain of thought; the base of parallel test-time scaling.
numbers: Absolute gains: GSM8K +17.9%, SVAMP +11.0%, AQuA +12.2%, StrategyQA +6.4%, ARC-challenge +3.9% (headline models, many sampled paths).
limits: Needs a single countable answer. Gains shrink for weaker models and open-ended tasks.
agent_relevance: Baseline parallel method; cheap when answers are short.

source: Yue et al. (2025) Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model?
finding: At large k, base models reach higher pass@k than their RLVR-trained versions. RL makes sampling more efficient at k=1 but adds few new reasoning paths; the capability boundary may narrow. Distillation can add new ones.
numbers: pass@1 higher for RL models; pass@256 higher for base models, across math, code and visual reasoning; six RLVR algorithms perform similarly. Qwen2.5-7B/14B/32B base models among those used.
limits: Capability proxy is pass@k with a verifier; later work may find exceptions with longer RL (not checked).
agent_relevance: Test-time sampling can recover what training sharpened away; for new solutions use diversity, not a single trained mode.

source: Snell et al. (2024), FLOPs-matched comparison by difficulty (Fig. 1 text)
finding: Against a 14x larger pretrained model, the gain from test-time compute is positive on easy bins and negative on hard bins, and larger when inference demand is low.
numbers: Figure 1 labels include +27.8%, +21.6%, +16.7%, +11.8% on easy/mid cases and losses from -11.9% down to -52.9% on hard cases, depending on the inference-to-pretraining token ratio. Read from PDF figure text; exact bin mapping not checked.
limits: Numbers extracted from figure text; labels partly unclear.
agent_relevance: Hard items: extra test-time compute is a poor buy for a small model; route them to a stronger model, a tool or a human.

source: Gema et al. (2025), controlled vs natural overthinking
finding: Two ways to lengthen thinking were compared: controlled (set a budget) and natural (the model's own length). Controlled shows stronger degradation for Claude Opus 4 and R1; natural is noisier.
numbers: Misleading Math: Opus 4 near perfect with little reasoning, about 80% at long budgets; o3 shows positive scaling across distractor counts; R1 stays within confidence intervals in the natural setting.
limits: The same model can look different depending on how length is varied.
agent_relevance: Do not assume forced length and natural length behave the same when designing a budget knob.

source: Qu et al. (2025) Scaling Test-Time Compute Without Verification or RL is Suboptimal
finding: Theory and experiments: fine-tuning with verifier-based methods (RL or search) scales better than distilling search traces (verifier-free). The gap widens as budget grows.
numbers: Shown on didactic and math tasks with 3B/8B/32B models; s1 (distillation) compared with best-of-N verifier search; gap grows with test-time budget.
limits: Holds under heterogeneous correct traces and a non-sharp reward distribution (anti-concentration condition). Author list taken from memory, not checked.
agent_relevance: If we scale compute at inference we need a verifier signal, not only more free-form thought.

source: Wu et al. (2025) Does Thinking More Always Help? Understanding Test-Time Scaling in Reasoning Models
finding: Extending thinking (Wait, rethink) first raises accuracy then lowers it. A simple probabilistic model says extra thinking raises output variance, which looks like gain but is not better reasoning. Parallel thinking within the same budget does better.
numbers: Up to 20% higher accuracy for parallel thinking with majority vote versus extended thinking at equal budget; tested on GSM-8K, MATH-500, AIME 2024 with forced thinking-token counts.
quote: Does thinking more at test-time truly lead to better reasoning?
limits: The variance explanation is a model, not a direct test. Open reasoning models only.
agent_relevance: Prefer a few independent attempts over one very long chain at equal tokens; cap sequential extension.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking
finding: On controllable puzzles, reasoning models beat plain models only at medium complexity. At low complexity plain models do as well or better; at high complexity both collapse. Reasoning effort even drops near the collapse point.
numbers: Three regimes (low, medium, high complexity). Accuracy falls to near zero beyond a model-specific complexity (Tower of Hanoi N up to 10+ disks and other puzzles); tokens used rise with complexity then fall at the collapse threshold despite spare budget.
limits: Critics argue output-length limits and puzzle format explain part of the collapse (critiques not read here).
agent_relevance: Matches the S0 gate idea: easy items need no thinking; hopeless items should be escalated rather than thought about longer.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: o1-like models waste tokens on easy items; later solutions after the first correct one add little. Training on shorter self-generated answers cuts tokens without losing accuracy.
numbers: For 2+3, o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models; the method cuts token output by 48.6% on MATH500 with QwQ-32B-Preview while keeping accuracy.
quote: consumed 1,953% more tokens than conventional models
limits: Efficiency metrics are defined by the authors; mainly QwQ and similar.
agent_relevance: Supports an explicit S0 fast path: answer easy items directly.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025) DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning
finding: RL with verifiable rewards makes thinking length grow by itself and lifts AIME. Majority voting adds a further gain.
numbers: R1-Zero AIME 2024 pass@1 rises from 15.6% to 77.9% during training; with majority voting 86.7%. R1 majority voting: 79.8% to 86.7%.
limits: Length growth is partly a training effect; later work questions whether longer is causal.
agent_relevance: Both axes (long thought and voting) stack; budget is a trained behaviour, not only a prompt.

source: Xu et al. (2025) What, How, Where, and How Well? A Survey on Test-Time Scaling / Test-Time Compute (arXiv 2501.02497)
finding: Organises test-time compute from System-1 models (parameter updating, input modification, representation editing, output calibration) to System-2 (repeated sampling, self-correction, tree search).
numbers: Survey; no new numbers. Only abstract and front matter were checked for this line.
limits: Strength depends on the cited papers; many claims come from math and code. Title and author list not fully verified.
agent_relevance: Map of method families; shows test-time compute is more than one technique.

source: Levi (2024) A Simple Model of Inference Scaling Laws
finding: A memorisation-style statistical model explains why coverage (pass@k) follows a power law in the number of trials and defines an inference loss with power-law decay.
numbers: Tested on a simple generative model; predictions agree with empirical coverage curves in the controlled setting.
limits: Toy setting; not tested on frontier LLMs.
agent_relevance: Predicts diminishing returns: cost per extra point rises sharply.

source: Synthesis: parallel versus sequential scaling (Muennighoff 2025; Wu 2025; Snell 2024)
finding: Findings conflict: s1 finds sequential forcing beats majority vote; Wu et al. find parallel beats extended thinking at equal budget; Snell finds it depends on difficulty. A likely resolution: the winner depends on difficulty and model (an interpretation, not tested in one study).
numbers: s1: sequential reaches AIME 57%; Wu: parallel up to +20% over extended thinking; Snell: sequential for easy, parallel or search for hard.
limits: Different models, benchmarks and budgets. No single test crosses all three.
agent_relevance: Do not hard-code one mode; choose by difficulty (G12).

source: Synthesis: coverage versus selection (Brown 2024; Chen 2024)
finding: Coverage rises with samples while voting accuracy stalls or even falls, because selection, not generation, is the bottleneck.
numbers: MATH Llama-3-8B: coverage 98.44% at 10,000 samples vs 41.41% for voting or reward model; Chen et al. show vote accuracy can fall with more calls.
limits: Two different setups; the link is an interpretation.
agent_relevance: Invest in the selector; coverage numbers overstate usable gain.

source: Synthesis: the base model's reach (Yue 2025; Brown 2024)
finding: Both say the base model already contains many correct paths at high k. Test-time sampling finds them; RL mostly shifts probability onto them.
numbers: Yue: base pass@256 above the RL model; Brown: coverage near 98% on MATH at 10,000 samples.
limits: Different models and metrics.
agent_relevance: Capability ceiling is not default accuracy; a scaffold can lift default toward the ceiling with good selection.

source: Stroebl et al. (2024), cost of false positives and retry count
finding: With a cost for returning a wrong accepted answer, the optimal retry count falls. Even with infinite compute, the best K can be zero for weak models.
numbers: On HumanEval+ the optimal number of attempts is often under 10; for weak models the false-positive risk can outweigh the gain.
limits: Coding benchmark; the utility cost is assumed by the authors.
agent_relevance: Add a cost-of-wrong-answer term to the budget rule.

source: Snell et al. (2024), PRM search methods compared
finding: Three PRM search methods compared: best-of-N, beam search, lookahead search (lookahead costs more per step). The process reward model consistently beat an outcome reward model.
numbers: Text: beam width and lookahead depth tuned on MATH; PRM consistently outperformed ORM. Crossover budgets not extracted.
limits: Details of the beam-versus-best-of-N crossover were not read closely.
agent_relevance: Step-level search needs a step-level verifier; otherwise use best-of-N.

source: Gema et al. (2025), regression task with spurious features and few-shot
finding: On a regression task with spurious features, models shift from sensible priors to spurious correlations as they think longer; 16-shot examples change the pattern.
numbers: Compared 0-shot and 16-shot for Claude Opus 4 on a student-grade regression across budgets; exact numbers not extracted.
limits: Synthetic task; exact deltas not read.
agent_relevance: Give worked examples to anchor long reasoning.
